The Conclave

An irreverent online literary publication that treats submissions as sins and rejections as forgiveness.

Submit and Be Forgiven

What I did

  • Brand concept, tagline, and voice
  • All site copy
  • Pen-in-cross logo
  • Site design and build in Carrd
  • Sourced all stock images

The idea

Reimagine the aesthetic of religion as a shamelessly ironic, comedic space where every submission is a sacrament. "Like our own church, just hotter."

The system

Five sections (Sacrament, Confession, Submission, Conclave, Mission), a monthly contest built from reader confessions, and a rotating Pope of the Month who judges them.

Look and feel

Content note: the publication is intentionally irreverent and adult. These excerpts are my own copy only, lightly selected.

Mission

"Judgment pervades every crevice of society; but at The Conclave, we accept anything and everything shameful and embrace it."

Staff bio

"Kind of like Mother Mary if she liked to party."

Donations

"And like all good churches, we love guilting you into giving us your money. We deserve it more than you and we'll put it to really good use."

Guidelines / The Confessional

"Confessionals must be nonfiction and truthful. Lying is a sin, you know."
"We'll see it when we see it. And then you'll see it when you see it."

Guidelines / The Sacrament

"There is no word limit and no restrictions on submissions. However, a $10 indulgence is required per submission. You’ll need it, you’re a sinner."

Guidelines / Contest

"Contest winners will be announced on the first of every month along with the new theme, and each winner is offered a position as guest judge for the following contest. Winners will receive a prize of $11. Greed is also a sin."

Confessional replies

The Pope gasps: "Shamelessly disgusting! Frat party turned secret lesbian sorority orgy foiled by the woes of early onset alcoholism is an excellent contest prompt. Forgiven!"

Astrology deck

A persuasive early college presentation arguing that astrology deserves more respect than it gets, written in a playful voice that sounds like a friend making a case over coffee.

Astrology: A Conspiracy?... Or Not?

Highlights from the 12-slide deck: three slide titles and selected copy.

Slide titles

Real or Not?
They Believed in Astrology!
Fine, Here's Some Science

Selected excerpts by slide

"While modern science seems to disagree completely with this notion, I am here to argue the opposite (astrology is real for me, ok). The moon can determine our mood! Some planetary positions may even determine the course of our whole generation! And the folklore of our predecessors seems to agree…"Slide 3, Thesis
"As any woman who has had to interact with a man recently will know, astrology has recently become a subject of ridicule and debate. It makes you wonder: would that guy on Tinder have called Ptolemy and his study stupid? Was Alexander the Great a fool compared to, I don't know, frat Brad? I digress, but in any case, the recent social climate surrounding the astrology is very black and white (either you believe in it or you don't)."Slide 4, Real or Not?
"I believe in science fully. Evolution is the coolest thing ever and I love that we don't have, like, the Black Plague anymore."Slide 10, Fine, Here's Some Science
"Anyways, why wouldn’t we know a little something about what the heavens are saying? We are made of the same star dust, after all."Slide 11, Conclusion

Book review

A graduate-level review that argues for reading beyond the American bestseller list, and uses one novel to make the case. Written in a polished voice.

Down the Rabbit Hole? No, Down the Elevator Shaft

On Elevator in Sài Gòn by Thuận, translated by Nguyễn An Lý

Selected excerpts

When we choose a book to read, we tend to unapologetically gravitate towards what we know. In the western world, easy-to-digest romance fantasy, marketable self-help, and the inspirational memoir dominate our American tastes.

But, I implore readers to shift their attention away from their own market, to pick up the modest 170-page English translation of a "detective thriller, historical romance, immigrant experience" novel.

…

Best known for her award-winning novel Chinatown, prolific Vietnamese author Thuận returns with her newest release, Elevator in Sài Gòn, a novel both personally intricate and politically satirical, translated by Nguyễn An Lý.

…

I picked up the little novel and leafed through it, considering the privilege of being able to indulge in a banned book, and how it had been so conveniently translated to English. Thuận's book checked all of my boxes, and offered a deliciously enticing new form of storytelling. A detective-type novel that bounces between Hanoi and Saigon, currently banned in Vietnam? The mythos of the book itself was irresistible.

…

The narrator pokes fun at her family, the roles they played during the war, and the war itself all while maintaining a thriller-like sense of tension beneath the satirical humor.

…

The novel is not a comedy, but the narrator is immensely human, and Thuận captures the deeply human experience of absurdity with ease.

Closing line

It would be a disservice to ourselves as readers to not search beyond the horizon: the translated, the foreign, and the banned.
